---
guardian_issue:
  id: "ISSUE-CAPACITY-GUARD-DTO"
  title: "capacity_ledger: ReserveCapacityOutput::guard is always None — the DTO advertises an RAII handle that does not exist"
  epic: "capacity ledger"
  component: "CapacityLedger"
  module: "capacity-ledger"
  status: planned
  priority: medium
  dependencies:
    - "ADR-018 capacity ledger (the seam settles by reservation id)"
    - "ADR-008 RAII reservation pattern (the pattern this field claims to offer)"
    - "Contract freeze ISSUE-CONTRACT-FREEZE (the DTO is frozen; this is a contract change)"

  intent: |
    Resolve a false contract. ReserveCapacityOutput.guard is documented as "RAII handle
    owning the reservation... dropping it without committing releases the hold", but
    CapacityLedgerServiceImpl::reserve hard-codes guard: None, so the field is never
    populated and ReservationGuardImpl is constructed only inside its own tests. There are
    two competing ownership designs in the code (by-id settlement in the service vs a
    drop-releasing guard), and only one of them is wired. Pick one, make the DTO honest,
    and stop implying a release-on-drop guarantee that the code does not provide.

  in_scope:
    - "Decide the ownership model: who owns the Grant — the service registry or the caller's guard"
    - "Make ReserveCapacityOutput stop advertising a handle it never returns"
    - "Either bring ReservationGuardImpl into production use, or delete it"
    - "Keep by-id commit/release working (the dispatch seam and the HTTP adapter both use it)"
    - "Update the DTO doc comment, the module doc and the seam's cross-reference"
    - "Retain release-on-drop semantics somewhere real (service teardown), or state plainly that leases are the only backstop"

  out_of_scope:
    - "Changing the HTTP wire shape (the field is #[serde(skip)]; see Wire impact below)"
    - "Changing lease semantics or the atomic reserve transaction"
    - "The dispatch seam's reserve/commit/release ordering (already correct)"

  affected_layers:
    domain:
      - "None (Grant ownership is unchanged in the domain)"
    application:
      - "Modified: dto/mod.rs — ReserveCapacityOutput.guard removed or re-typed"
      - "Modified: service_impl.rs — the grant/guard registry, take_grant, commit, release"
      - "Modified: guard_impl.rs — either used in production or deleted"
    infrastructure:
      - "Modified: http.rs — decodes ReserveCapacityOutput; already ignores the field"
    api:
      - "None on the wire; Rust API consumers of ReserveCapacityOutput are affected"

  canonical_references:
    - module: ".pi/architecture/modules/capacity-ledger.md#reservationguard"
    - adr:
        - ".pi/architecture/decisions/ADR-018-distributed-capacity-ledger.md"
        - ".pi/architecture/decisions/ADR-008-raii-budget-reservation.md"
    - evidence: "engine/src/capacity_ledger/application/dto/mod.rs:64-67"
    - evidence: "engine/src/capacity_ledger/application/service_impl.rs:96-100"
    - evidence: "engine/src/capacity_ledger/application/service_impl.rs:17-18"
    - evidence: "engine/src/capacity_ledger/application/guard_impl.rs:226,240,258 (tests only)"

  acceptance_criteria:
    - "No public DTO field documents a guarantee the implementation does not provide"
    - "ReservationGuardImpl has either a production caller or zero references (no test-only type in the public API)"
    - "Exactly one owner of a Grant at any time — no double-settle path exists"
    - "By-id commit and release still work (the dispatch seam's reachability test still passes)"
    - "Release-on-drop is either real (guards dropped with the service) or explicitly disclaimed in the docs"
    - "The frozen-DTO change is recorded: the field is #[serde(skip)], absent from every response schema, and nowhere read by a caller — so this is a Rust-API change, not a wire change"
    - "validate-architecture.sh and validate-canonical.sh pass"

  validators:
    - ci
    - tests
    - architecture
    - canonical

  implementation_notes: |
    - Recommended: the service owns the guards. Store Box<dyn ReservationGuard> in the
      registry keyed by ReservationId; reserve inserts; commit(id)/release(id) take from it
      and settle through the guard; dropping the service drops every outstanding guard and
      releases it. Then remove ReserveCapacityOutput.guard (it cannot be handed out without
      breaking by-id settlement) and ReservationGuardImpl becomes production-live. This keeps
      the by-id API, restores RAII at service lifetime, and removes the double owner.
    - Do NOT hand out the guard while the service also holds the grant: that is two owners of
      one reservation and a guaranteed double-settle attempt.
    - Do NOT just correct the comment. The type would stay dead and the next contributor would
      re-derive the same confusion.
    - The seam currently settles by id and documents why (service_impl.rs:552); that note must
      be updated with whatever this issue decides.
    - Because #[serde(skip)] excludes the field from the wire, no client can be relying on it;
      no SDK catalog change is needed.

  file_changes:
    - "modify: engine/src/capacity_ledger/application/dto/mod.rs"
    - "modify: engine/src/capacity_ledger/application/service_impl.rs"
    - "modify or delete: engine/src/capacity_ledger/application/guard_impl.rs"
    - "modify: engine/src/capacity_ledger/infrastructure/http.rs (if the type changes)"
    - "modify: engine/src/execution_engine/application/service_impl.rs (seam cross-reference)"
    - "modify: engine/.pi/architecture/modules/capacity-ledger.md"

  pipeline_steps:
    - implement
    - validate
    - create-mr
    - merge
---

# ISSUE-CAPACITY-GUARD-DTO — `ReserveCapacityOutput::guard` is always `None`

## Intent

The DTO advertises a release-on-drop handle. The service never returns one. Resolve the
contradiction rather than documenting it away.

## Evidence

| claim | evidence |
|---|---|
| the field promises release-on-drop | `dto/mod.rs:64-67` — *"RAII handle owning the reservation… dropping it without committing releases the hold"* |
| it is never populated | `service_impl.rs:96-100` — `guard: None`, hard-coded |
| the code knows | `service_impl.rs:17-18` — *"RAII guard wiring lands in ISSUE-CAPACITY-LEDGER-8; `reserve` currently returns `guard: None`"* |
| the guard type is production-dead | `ReservationGuardImpl::new` appears **only** at `guard_impl.rs:226,240,258`, all inside `#[cfg(test)]` |
| the service settles by id instead | `take_grant(&ReservationId)` + the `grants` registry, used by `commit`/`release` |

So there are **two ownership designs** and only the by-id one is wired.

## Why it matters

A caller who reads the DTO contract will write:

```rust
if let Some(guard) = out.guard { /* rely on drop to release */ }
```

That branch is unreachable. The caller concludes either that no hold exists (it does) or that
dropping releases it (it does not) — and capacity then strands until the lease expires. The
documented guarantee is the opposite of the behaviour, which is the same defect class as the
unwired port and the dormant gate: *the shape of the API promises something the code does not do*.

## Wire impact: none

- The field is `#[serde(skip)]`, so it is absent from every serialized payload.
- No JSON schema names `ReserveCapacityOutput` (`interfaces/http/mod.rs` uses the name only as a
  Rust-side `response_schema` label for `EndpointContract`).
- `HttpLedger` decodes `ReserveCapacityOutput` and already reads only `.reservation`, never
  `.guard`.
- Therefore removing the field is a **Rust API change, not a wire change** — no SDK catalog
  change and no client impact.

## Decision required

**Option A (recommended) — the service owns the guards; remove the DTO field.**
Registry holds `Box<dyn ReservationGuard>` keyed by `ReservationId`. `reserve` inserts;
`commit(id)`/`release(id)` take and settle through the guard; dropping the service drops every
outstanding guard and releases it. By-id APIs keep working (the seam and the HTTP adapter need
them), `ReservationGuardImpl` becomes live, and RAII applies at service lifetime — strictly
better than per-call.

**Option B — hand out the guard and retire the by-id APIs.** Correct RAII per reservation, but
it breaks the HTTP adapter (a remote reservation cannot return a local guard) and requires the
seam to hold guards. Larger, and the HTTP adapter must keep the by-id path anyway.

**Option C — keep the behaviour, delete the field, state the lease is the only backstop.**
Smallest change; honest. Loses the immediate-release property on teardown.

All three are acceptable; **doing nothing is not**, because the contract currently lies.

## Acceptance Criteria

See front matter. The load-bearing ones: no DTO field promises an unimplemented guarantee, no
public type is production-dead, exactly one owner per `Grant`, and the dispatch seam's
reachability test still passes.

## Notes

This does not block anything: the seam already settles by id and documents why
(`engine/src/execution_engine/application/service_impl.rs:552`). It is a correctness-of-contract
fix, not a functional gap.
title: capacity_ledger: ReserveCapacityOutput::guard is always None — the DTO advertises an RAII handle that does not exist

## Update — 2026-10-18 (still accurate; the recommended path now exists)

Re-verified: the placeholder comment is still present at
`engine/src/enforcement/application/enforcer_impl.rs:173` —
*"Per-tool call count tracking is reserved for a future implementation."* No code path counts
per-tool calls; the comment advertises a capability that does not exist.

**What changed:** the "express it as a ledger-governed resource" option is no longer
hypothetical. The capacity-ledger seam landed in `a861e2a8` and demonstrates the exact pattern
a real per-tool counter would use: declare a resource with a hard limit, claim an amount per
dispatch, commit on success, release on failure, fail closed on any ledger error. There is now
a worked example (`tests/capacity_ledger_composition_e2e.rs`) instead of a design sketch.

**Decision (unchanged):** needed → implement through the ledger seam, not as a third bespoke
counter; not needed → delete the placeholder and any stub.

**Acceptance (unchanged):** no comment in `enforcement` advertises an unimplemented capability.
If implemented, it is concurrency-tested.

Still ordered after #1017 — the authoritative-mechanism decision should land first so this does
not add a third way to count.

---

# ISSUE-ENFORCEMENT-PER-TOOL-CALL-TRACKING

## Intent

Either implement per-tool call counting properly (via the ledger) or delete the placeholder.

## Evidence

`enforcer_impl.rs:173` — *"Per-tool call count tracking is reserved for a future implementation."*

## Why it matters

A comment that advertises a future capability reads, to a maintainer, as a capability that
exists. This project has already had one such case (`precondition` reachability) and resolved it
by making the wiring explicit. Do the same, at this much smaller scale.

## Acceptance Criteria

No unimplemented guarantee is advertised in enforcement. If built, it is ledger-governed and
concurrency-tested.
title: enforcement: resolve the 'reserved for a future implementation' per-tool call counter

## Update — 2026-10-18 (dependency LANDED; the decision is now actionable)

The facts remain true, but the blocker is gone.

**Dependency satisfied.** The capacity-ledger dispatch seam landed in `a861e2a8`
(`feat(capacity-ledger): wire the seam into the dispatch path`). The engine now performs
reserve → dispatch → commit/release on the real `run_dispatch_loop` path, armed from
`.rigorix/capacity.toml` by `CapacitySetup::from_env` and attached at all three production
composition roots (CLI, MCP host, GitHub Action). Proof: `tests/capacity_ledger_composition_e2e.rs`
drives the real loop, and the over-cap case **fails if the seam call is removed** (verified by
removal).

**Re-verified evidence, today:**

| fact | evidence (current) |
|---|---|
| generic resource concept | `enforcement/domain/config.rs:513` — `ResourceBudget { resource, soft_warning_threshold, hard_limit, current_usage }` |
| it is a counter | `enforcement/application/enforcer_impl.rs:109-129` — `usage_ratio`, `current_usage >= hard_limit` |
| no reservation concept | `grep reserve engine/src/enforcement` → zero hits |
| **still zero integration** | `grep -rc 'capacity_ledger' engine/src/enforcement` → **0 files** |
| blast radius (grep) | **31 references across 9 files** |
| blast radius (graph) | 38 upstream symbols, MEDIUM risk, 7 direct (mostly tests) |

So there are now **two working mechanisms for "a limited resource" and nothing connects
them**: `ResourceBudget` counts and compares; `CapacityLedger` reserves atomically and is
wired into dispatch. Exactly the ambiguity this issue exists to remove.

**Decision required (unchanged):** view over the ledger / deprecated / explicitly scoped to
non-contested limits. Two considerations that are now concrete rather than hypothetical:

- `ResourceBudget` is per-run in-memory and cannot see other executions; the ledger can. For
  anything contested, the counter is not merely redundant — it is **wrong**.
- Non-contested per-run limits (tool calls, timeout) are legitimately not ledger-shaped, so a
  blanket "port everything to the ledger" is also wrong.

A likely landing zone: keep `ResourceBudget` for per-execution, non-contested budget keys and
state that explicitly in its doc comment; route anything whose limit is shared across
executions through the capacity ledger. Either way, **the doc must say which is which**.

**Acceptance (unchanged):** exactly one authoritative mechanism per resource, stated in docs
and enforced in code; existing enforcement tests pass; do not delete `ResourceBudget` blindly.

---

# ISSUE-RESOURCE-BUDGET-COUNTER-SUPERSEDED

## Intent

Remove the ambiguity between the existing generic counter and the new reservation primitive
before two teams adopt different answers.

## Evidence

| fact | evidence |
|---|---|
| generic resource concept | `config.rs:513` — `ResourceBudget { resource: String, ... }` |
| it is a counter | `enforcer_impl.rs:109-129` — `usage_ratio`, `current_usage >= hard_limit` |
| no reservation concept exists there | `grep reserve engine/src/enforcement` → zero hits |
| impact | 38 upstream symbols, MEDIUM risk, 7 direct (mostly tests) |

## In Scope

Decide the relationship, implement it, document which is authoritative.

## Out of Scope

Threshold semantics for non-contested resources; the ledger implementation.

## Notes

The type stays; the duplication goes.
title: enforcement: ResourceBudget is a counter, not a reservation — supersede it via the capacity ledger

## Update — 2026-10-18 (scope broadened: there are now TWO dead persistence ports)

The first is unchanged and still accurate:

| claim | evidence | status |
|---|---|---|
| the port declares persistence | `budget_tracking/infrastructure/repository/mod.rs` | still true |
| nothing calls it | `llm_budget_impl.rs` — **0** repository references | still true |
| only tests call it | `record_reservation` — **0** production callers | still true |
| only one adapter exists | `in_memory_budget_repository.rs` | still true |

**Second instance, found while wiring the capacity ledger:**

`engine/src/capacity_ledger/infrastructure/repository/mod.rs:29` declares
`CapacityLedgerRepository` (put_spec / get_spec / put_reservation / get_reservation /
find_by_idempotency_key / list_reservations / exposure) — a persistence seam.

- **implementations: NONE** (`grep -rn 'impl CapacityLedgerRepository'` → 0)
- **production references: NONE** outside its own file

So the capacity ledger now has a *working* port (`CapacityLedger` → `InProcessLedger` /
`HttpLedger`, wired into the dispatch path in `a861e2a8`) **and** a second dead persistence
port next to it. This matters for the decision below: **"fold it into the capacity ledger"
is not a fix while the capacity ledger's own repository seam is equally unreferenced** — it
would move the dead port, not remove it.

**Decision required (now four options):**
1. delete `LlmBudgetRepository` and keep in-memory budgets explicitly ephemeral;
2. wire a durable adapter for budgets;
3. fold budgets into the capacity ledger **after** resolving `CapacityLedgerRepository`
   (use it for the in-process/HTTP adapters, or delete it);
4. delete both dead ports and state plainly that persistence is the enterprise service's job
   (which is what the shipped architecture actually did: `HttpLedger` talks to the enterprise
   ledger service; nothing in the OSS engine persists capacity locally).

**Acceptance (strengthened):** no trait method in either module lacks a production caller;
if `CapacityLedgerRepository` is deleted, `InProcessLedger`/`HttpLedger` must not be relying on
it (verified by build + tests); the chosen option is recorded in the module docs.

---

# ISSUE-BUDGET-REPOSITORY-PORT-UNWIRED

## Intent

A declared persistence port that nothing persists through is an active hazard: a reader
reasonably concludes that budgets are durable. Resolve it deliberately.

## Evidence

| claim | evidence |
|---|---|
| the port declares persistence | `repository/mod.rs` — `save`, `record_reservation`, `record_commit`, `list` |
| nothing calls it | `llm_budget_impl.rs` has **zero** references to the repository |
| only tests call it | graph: `record_reservation` → *"Called by: test_budget_round_trip"* |
| only one adapter exists | `in_memory_budget_repository.rs` is the sole implementation |

## Decision required

Delete, fold into the capacity ledger, or wire a durable adapter. Record which, and why.

## Acceptance Criteria

No trait method without a production caller. If kept, a reachability test — not unit coverage.
title: persistence ports: LlmBudgetRepository and CapacityLedgerRepository are both declared and neither has a caller

## Update — 2026-10-18 (re-verified against code)

**Part 2 (release-notes home) is DELIVERED.** `CHANGELOG.md` exists (1224 lines, Keep a
Changelog, backfilled to 1.8.0) and is gated by `.pi/scripts/validate-docs.sh`
(newest entry must equal `engine/Cargo.toml`). Release notes are out of the main README.
Dependency #1012 is closed and delivered.

**Part 1 (verified comparables) is NOT delivered, and the rewrite left a new defect.**

- The comparison table is gone (correct — it compared Rigorix to the agents it governs).
- **`README.md:271` now dangles:** it says *"See the comparison note below"* and **no such
  section exists** — the next heading is `## Interfaces`. Verified:
  `grep -n -i 'comparison note\|## compar' README.md` returns only that one line.
  This is a broken cross-reference shipped by #1014 and must be fixed either way.

**Recommended content when this is picked up** (from the research pass): replace the old
"you vs. the agents" framing with the six **credential-binding failure modes** (scope,
argument, temporal, tool, delegation, semantic) as the comparison dimensions, sourced and
dated. Rigorix's differentiators map onto those modes rather than onto named competitors,
which keeps the table verifiable and out of the wrong category.

**Still excluded by the inclusion rule:** anything a reader cannot adopt today without a
sales conversation (enterprise-tier comparables), and any competitor cell that cannot be
sourced and dated → "not established".

**Acceptance (unchanged, plus one):** every competitor cell sourced + dated or
"not established"; the table is not in the wrong category; **no dangling cross-reference
remains in README.md**.

---

# ISSUE-POSITIONING-AND-RELEASE-NOTES

## Defect 1 — the comparison table is a category error

The README compares Rigorix against **Claude Code, Copilot/Cursor, Aider, SWE-Agent**.
Those are the agents Rigorix governs. The README says so in its own words:

> "Rigorix isn't a separate agent — it's a governance layer underneath yours."

Putting them side by side contradicts the thesis and makes Rigorix read like a
worse agent instead of a different layer.

## The real comparables (researched 2026-10-14)

**Same category:**

| product | their positioning | why it is relevant |
|---|---|---|
| **Cordum** | "The Action Firewall for AI Agents" | policy + approval + redacted audit evidence *before* execution, in front of Claude Code / MCP / shell; action-hash approval; source-available core |
| **Mault** | "Governance for Coding Agents" | deterministic rules keystroke→merge, **signed record of every action**, explicitly "no LLM in the enforcement path", local |
| **APERION** | "Runtime AI Governance for Enterprise Agents" | on-prem; stops actions exceeding authority; record bound to a human owner; `AperionAI/shield` is a free local guardrail with PreToolUse hooks and a demo GIF |
| **microsoft/agent-governance-toolkit** | policy enforcement + zero-trust identity + sandboxing | MIT, ~6.4k stars, 10/10 OWASP Agentic Top 10 — the most credible open-source neighbour |
| AGCP.ai · LangGuard · ControlTower OS | "deterministic runtime AI governance" | same vocabulary; verify individually first |

**Adjacent, not rivals:** Microsoft **Agent Hooks** (an open governance *contract* —
Rigorix should aim to be compatible, not competitive), **OPA/Styra** (static
request authorization), **agentsh / OS sandboxes** (syscall-level, no semantics).

**Wrong category, must not appear:** **Credo AI** (AI governance/compliance
platform), **Opaque** (confidential computing), **SICKR.ai** (workforce governance).

## Where Rigorix is verifiably better

Each of these is traceable to a shipped artifact — no others may be claimed:

| # | differentiator | artifact |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Open-source polyglot verifiers** — competitors hand you their record; Rigorix hands you the verifier | `rigorix-verifier` on crates.io / npm / PyPI; Go + Java in `rigorix-sdk`; GitHub Action |
| 2 | **Verification by re-derivation, not by signature** | spec §4.3.1 |
| 3 | **Moment separation** (plan / approval / dispatch) | ADR-017 |
| 4 | **Cross-run identity-bound records** with an anchor | ADR-016 |
| 5 | **Canonical effect keys** (value-identity resolution) | `eff:` keys in the envelope |
| 6 | **A stated claim ceiling** — never asserts present standing | spec, NC-4 |

## The rules that keep the table honest

1. **Source and date every competitor cell.** A table without a date is wrong
   within a month.
2. **Unverifiable cell → "not established."** No inferred weaknesses. "We could not
   establish X" is fine; "they lack X" without a source is not.
3. **Never claim a row Rigorix cannot itself demonstrate.**
4. **State what the table is not.** It is not a benchmark; no independent
   comparative evaluation exists (L1/L2/L3 claim ceilings).

## Defect 2 — release notes need a home

```
CHANGELOG.md         ABSENT
release history      GitHub Releases only (v1.10.0, v1.9.5, v1.9.4, v1.9.3, …)
who generates it     .github/workflows/release.yml -> "Generate changelog"
```

Pick **`CHANGELOG.md`** at the root (Keep a Changelog, newest first, linked to the
GitHub Release) or `docs/releases/`. It must be in-repo, and it must **not** be in
the main README — the README links to it. Backfill `1.9.x` from the existing
Releases, and consider having the release workflow append automatically so the two
cannot drift.

## Acceptance Criteria

| # | Criterion | Validator |
|---|-----------|-----------|
| 1 | No coding assistant listed as a competitor | review |
| 2 | Every competitor cell sourced + dated; unsourced reads "not established" | review |
| 3 | Every Rigorix advantage traceable to code or spec | `validate-canonical.sh` |
| 4 | Release notes live in-repo and are not in the README | `validate-docs.sh` |
| 5 | Changelog format chosen and documented | review |
| 6 | The table states what it does not establish | review |

## Implementation

> **Agent:** Re-verify every competitor claim at implementation time — this research
> is dated 2026-10-14 and competitors ship weekly. If you cannot source a cell,
> write "not established". Do not spin an unfavourable row; remove it.

### Steps

1. Re-read each competitor's site/repo; capture the exact wording and the date
2. Rebuild the table on the six verifiable dimensions; mark unknowns explicitly
3. Delete the coding-assistant columns entirely
4. Choose the changelog home; create it; backfill from the GitHub Releases
5. Link the README to the changelog; remove any version list from the README
6. (Optional) wire the release workflow to append
7. Add the "what this table is not" note
title: Competitive positioning: replace the category-error comparison table, and give release notes a durable home
